paper.title: Clean Data Can Still Carry Backdoors: Support-Persistent Backdoors for Model Reuse
paper.summary: Traditional backdoor attacks inject artificial trigger patterns into training data, causing models to misclassify triggered inputs while maintaining normal behavior on clean samples. Since these artificial triggers are absent in clean datasets, standard knowledge distillation (KD) typically eliminates them, leading to the common belief that KD serves as an effective purification defense. In this paper, we propose DAR (Discover-and-Relabel), a support-persistent backdoor method that retains its behavior even after clean-data distillation. DAR identifies naturally abundant patterns in low-dimensional feature subspaces using subspace clustering and applies label-only poisoning to samples that inherently satisfy the discovered rule. At test time, the backdoor is activated by locally modifying the corresponding subspace of the target images. By instantiating spatial and frequency operators, DAR achieves attack accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art backdoor attacks in ImageNet classification and CLIP-based prompt tuning. Notably, DAR keeps attack success above 96% after clean KD and remains defense-resistant in practice. Project page: https://junhoo.me/backdoor

analysis.executive_summary: This work challenges the prevailing assumption that knowledge distillation effectively purges backdoor triggers by introducing DAR, a method that exploits natural data patterns rather than artificial triggers. It demonstrates that backdoors can remain highly effective (above 96% success rate) even after distillation, posing a significant risk to the safe reuse of pre-trained models in production environments.

paper.title: GNN-Guided Local Refinement for Efficient Layout Decomposition with DSA-MP
paper.summary: Multiple patterning lithography (MPL) has been widely used to improve lithography resolution in advanced nodes, but it faces cost limits as feature sizes shrink. Directed self-assembly (DSA) offers a cost-effective complement, extending the resolution of optical lithography to sub-10 nm and beyond. Integrating DSA into MPL (DSA-MP) further enhances the resolution of contact/via patterning. Nevertheless, growing design complexity exposes the limits of existing decomposition methods, which struggle to balance solution quality and runtime, and neglect edge-to-edge spacing constraints of DSA templates, compromising manufacturability. To address these issues, we introduce a new conflict graph model capturing the previously overlooked constraints and develop a local refinement strategy powered by the graph neural network, enabling efficient and scalable layout decomposition. Experiments demonstrate that our method achieves higher solution quality with faster convergence than state-of-the-art methods, while maintaining robustness across layout scales, design styles, technology nodes, and varying mask counts.

paper.title: Evaluating Inquiry Learning in LLM-Based Agents: Hypothesizing, Reasoning, and Exploration
paper.summary: Scientific inquiry involves iterative cycles of exploration, hypothesis generation, and reasoning over observations to uncover relationships in complex systems. Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in several components of this process, including inductive reasoning, hypothesis generation, and data analysis. However, prior work typically evaluates these abilities in isolation, leaving open how models integrate them across a full inquiry cycle. In this work, we introduce a framework for evaluating LLMs' inquiry capabilities in a unified, interactive setting. We extend the Countdown task to a mathematical environment where an agent probes the system by manipulating variables, collecting observations, and inferring relationships between them. This setup enables analysis of exploration strategies, causal discovery, and hypothesis refinement during inquiry. Across seven LLMs and multiple prompting strategies, our experiments reveal limited inherent inquiry capabilities and low success rates in discovering the underlying expressions. However, structured guidance inspired by educational scaffolding significantly improves performance. Our findings highlight current limitations of LLMs in strategic exploration and iterative hypothesis refinement, and show how simple guidance strategies developed for human learners in inquiry learning can support more effective inquiry behavior.
paper.comment: EMNLP 2026 (Findings)

analysis.problem_statement: The paper addresses the lack of unified evaluation frameworks for assessing how LLMs integrate exploration, hypothesis generation, and reasoning into a complete scientific inquiry cycle, rather than evaluating these skills in isolation.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Limited strategic exploration and iterative hypothesis refinement capabilities in LLMs within interactive, multi-step reasoning environments.
analysis.executive_summary: This work highlights a significant gap in current LLM capabilities, showing that models struggle to autonomously discover underlying mathematical relationships through iterative probing without external guidance. It demonstrates that while inherent inquiry skills are limited, applying educational scaffolding strategies can significantly enhance an agent's ability to perform causal discovery and refine hypotheses.

key_metrics.baseline: Unstructured prompting strategies across seven LLMs

technical_breakdown.architecture: A unified, interactive evaluation framework that simulates a scientific inquiry cycle involving variable manipulation, observation collection, and relationship inference.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Experiments are conducted across seven LLMs using multiple prompting strategies, with a specific focus on structured guidance inspired by educational scaffolding to support inquiry behavior.

paper.title: ESG-Kor: A Korean Dataset for ESG-related Information Extraction and Practical Use Cases
paper.summary: With the expansion of pre-trained language model usage in recent years, the importance of datasets for performing tasks in specialized domains has significantly increased. Therefore, we have built a Korean dataset called ESG-Kor to automatically extract Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) information, which has recently gained importance. ESG-Kor is a dataset consisting of a total of 118,946 sentences that extracted information on each ESG component from Korean companies' sustainability reports and manually labeled it according to objective rules provided by ESG evaluation agencies. To verify the effectiveness and applicability of the ESG-Kor dataset, classification performance was confirmed using several Korean pre-trained language models, and significant performance was obtained. Additionally, by extending the ESG classification model to documents of small and medium enterprises and extracting information based on ESG key issues and in-depth analysis, we demonstrated potential and practical use cases in the ESG field.
paper.comment: Published in Findings of EMNLP 2024

analysis.problem_statement: The lack of large-scale, manually labeled Korean datasets for extracting specific Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) information from corporate sustainability reports hinders the development of specialized NLP models for this domain.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Data scarcity and domain-specific labeling requirements for non-English financial and sustainability texts.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the critical gap in Korean NLP resources by introducing ESG-Kor, a dataset of 118,946 sentences derived from corporate sustainability reports. It demonstrates that pre-trained language models can effectively classify ESG components when trained on this specialized data, enabling practical applications for small and medium enterprises.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Classification performance of Korean pre-trained language models on ESG components
key_metrics.baseline: Korean pre-trained language models (unspecified specific baselines in abstract)

technical_breakdown.architecture: Pre-trained Korean Language Models (PLMs) fine-tuned for text classification tasks.

paper.title: Hierarchical Graph Convolutional Network Approach for Detecting Low-Quality Documents
paper.summary: Consistency within a document is a crucial feature indicative of its quality. Recently, within the vast amount of information produced across various media, there exists a significant number of low-quality documents that either lack internal consistency or contain content utterly unrelated to their headlines. Such low-quality documents induce fatigue in readers and undermine the credibility of the media source that provided them. Consequently, research to automatically detect these low-quality documents based on natural language processing is imperative. In this study, we introduce a hierarchical graph convolutional network (HGCN) that can detect internal inconsistencies within a document and incongruences between the title and body. Moreover, we constructed the Inconsistency Dataset, leveraging published news data and its meta-data, to train our model to detect document inconsistencies. Experimental results demonstrated that the HGCN achieved superior performance with an accuracy of 91.20% on our constructedInconsistency Dataset, outperforming other comparative models. Additionally, on the publicly available incongruent-related dataset, the proposed methodology demonstrated a performance of 92.00%, validating its general applicability. Finally, an ablation study further confirmed the significant impact of meta-data utilization on performance enhancement. We anticipate that our model can be universally applied to detect and filter low-quality documents in the real world.
paper.comment: Accepted at LREC-COLING 2024

analysis.problem_statement: The paper addresses the challenge of automatically detecting low-quality documents characterized by internal inconsistencies or incongruences between titles and body text.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Reliability and data quality in NLP pipelines, specifically the detection of semantic inconsistencies and hallucination-like content in generated or published text.
analysis.executive_summary: This work is significant for the current AI landscape as it provides a specialized method for filtering low-quality content, which is increasingly prevalent in automated media and LLM-generated outputs. By leveraging hierarchical graph structures to model document-level consistency, it offers a robust approach to maintaining information credibility and reducing reader fatigue.

paper.title: Asking Smarter Questions: Targeted Active Preference Learning for Underspecified Rewards
paper.summary: Reward learning typically assumes the human's input covers everything that matters for the task. In practice, humans can only attend to so much at once, so their teaching naturally captures some features---or aspects of the task---better than others. Prior work has shown how the robot can identify which features were poorly supervised directly from its teaching data. But the current solution is to ask the human to try again, putting the burden on someone who already struggled to convey those features. We propose shifting this burden to the robot. Our key insight is that the same information that tells the robot what it doesn't know can help it ask better questions. Preference queries offer a low-effort channel for resolving this uncertainty, but only if the robot knows where to direct them and the human knows what to attend to when answering. We act on this insight in two ways: we build an informed prior that targets preference queries at the features that need resolving, and we accompany each query with an explanation that focuses the human's attention on exactly those features. In simulation, the informed prior beats the standard active preference learning baseline by up to $30.8\%$ in the low-query regime, where reducing human effort matters most. In a user study, the informed prior and explanations each significantly improve reward recovery and amplify each other.
paper.comment: Accepted to the 10th Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL 2026), Austin, TX. 18 pages, 8 figures, 1 table

analysis.problem_statement: The paper addresses the inefficiency of standard active preference learning in robotics, where the burden of resolving underspecified rewards falls on humans who struggle to attend to all task features simultaneously.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Human-in-the-loop efficiency and the alignment gap caused by human cognitive limitations in providing comprehensive reward signals.
analysis.executive_summary: This work shifts the burden of resolving reward uncertainty from the human to the robot by using the robot's own knowledge gaps to target preference queries. By combining an informed prior for query selection with explanatory prompts that focus human attention, the method significantly reduces the number of queries needed to recover accurate rewards.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Reward recovery performance in low-query regimes
key_metrics.baseline: Standard active preference learning baseline

technical_breakdown.method: The system identifies poorly supervised features from teaching data to construct an informed prior that targets preference queries at specific uncertainties. Each query is accompanied by an explanation to direct human attention to the relevant features.
technical_breakdown.architecture: A two-component system consisting of an uncertainty-aware query selection module (informed prior) and a natural language explanation generator for human-robot interaction.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Uses preference queries as the interaction channel; leverages feature-level uncertainty estimation to guide query targeting; employs explanatory text to mitigate human attentional bias.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Not specified in the abstract; likely involves standard active learning loops with added natural language generation or templating for explanations.

paper.title: MAppPrint: Robust and Real-time Mobile App Fingerprinting via Traffic Behavior Correlation Graphs
paper.summary: Mobile apps have become ubiquitous in daily life. Despite communication encryption, app fingerprinting (AF) attacks can still enable adversaries to infer the apps in use by analyzing patterns of encrypted network traffic. However, existing AF attacks suffer from three critical limitations that hinder their practical effectiveness: (i) the inability to capture app-specific traffic dependencies, rendering traffic fingerprints fragile under dynamic networking conditions; (ii) the neglect of latency and throughput considerations, resulting in inefficient real-time user tracking; and (iii) the incapacity to handle mixed traffic generated by multi-app concurrency.   In this paper, we propose MAppPrint, a robust and real-time app fingerprinting framework. MAppPrint introduces a behavior-level traffic fingerprint, i.e., Traffic Behavior Correlation Graph (TBCG), which models app traffic by capturing unit traffic behaviors and their correlations, thereby providing reliable app fingerprints. To enable real-time fingerprinting, MAppPrint incorporates a fingerprint compression algorithm that transforms each TBCG into a compact graph by selectively aggregating redundant information. Furthermore, MAppPrint employs an unsupervised decomposition strategy to disentangle mixed traffic generated by multi-app concurrency, enabling unified identification of both single-app and multi-app traffic. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that MAppPrint achieves 4.9~13.9% improvement in AF precision and 3~6 times improvement in timeliness over state-of-the-art methods. Meanwhile, MAppPrint is robust in dynamic networking conditions, while achieving a throughput of 10.5 GB/s and a prediction latency of 0.68 seconds.
paper.comment: Accepted by NDSS 2027

analysis.problem_statement: Existing mobile app fingerprinting methods fail to capture app-specific traffic dependencies, ignore latency/throughput for real-time tracking, and cannot handle mixed traffic from concurrent app usage.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Lack of robustness and real-time efficiency in encrypted traffic analysis for identifying specific applications under dynamic and concurrent network conditions.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the critical security challenge of inferring user activity from encrypted traffic by introducing a graph-based model that captures behavioral correlations rather than just packet statistics. It enables real-time, high-throughput monitoring capable of distinguishing between single and multiple concurrent apps, significantly enhancing privacy protection and network security capabilities.

It applies a compression algorithm to create compact graph representations for speed and uses an unsupervised decomposition strategy to separate mixed traffic from concurrent apps.

paper.title: Subgraph Counting with Local Node Differential Privacy
paper.summary: We study the problem of approximately counting subgraphs under local node differential privacy (LNDP), a recently introduced model that enforces strong privacy guarantees in analyses of distributed social networks. We design a noninteractive $(\varepsilon,0)$-LNDP algorithm that, given any public $k$-node template graph $H$, counts occurrences of $H$ in a sensitive undirected $n$-node graph with additive error $O(n^{k-\frac{1}{2}}/\varepsilon^{k-1})$, for any constant $k$. We complement this algorithm with a lower bound showing that every noninteractive $(\varepsilon,δ)$-LNDP algorithm for counting copies of any $k$-node template graph with maximum degree greater than $1$ must have error $Ω(n^{k - \frac{1}{2}})$. Thus, our algorithm achieves optimal error for counting constant-size subgraphs, up to $\mathrm{poly}(1/\varepsilon)$ factors.   Our results substantially expand the types of network statistics known to be approximable under LNDP: prior work considered only functions of the degree distribution. In addition, our lower bound yields the first known $\mathrm{poly}(n)$ gap between central and local node differential privacy when accuracy is required for all input graphs. Previous separations either only involved $\mathrm{poly}(1/\varepsilon)$ factors or only applied to promise problems.
paper.comment: To appear at the ACM-SIAM Symposium on Discrete Algorithms (SODA) 2027

analysis.problem_statement: Approximately counting the occurrences of a given k-node template subgraph in a sensitive undirected graph under the local node differential privacy (LNDP) model.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Privacy-preserving graph analytics in distributed settings where strong privacy guarantees (LNDP) previously limited computable statistics to simple degree distributions, preventing the accurate estimation of complex structural properties like subgraph counts.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper establishes the first optimal noninteractive algorithm for subgraph counting under local node differential privacy, expanding the scope of private network analysis beyond degree distributions. It provides a tight lower bound that demonstrates a polynomial gap between central and local node differential privacy for general graph inputs, resolving a key theoretical separation in privacy-preserving data analysis.
